note: Optional readings and exercises from the second edition. Try the exercises before checking Appendix C for answers.

readings.title: Introduction to algorithms
readings.focus: Big O notation helps compare scanning sequence windows with enumerating every possible k-mer.

readings.title: Hash tables
readings.focus: Use keys and counts to organize repeated k-mers and avoid repeated scans.

readings.title: Greedy algorithms
readings.focus: For an extension, compare locally promising choices with a globally best motif set.

readings.title: Where to go next
readings.focus: Optional scalability extension: run independent randomized motif-search restarts in parallel, or count k-mers in separate reads and combine the counts by key.

motifs.connection: Count the 3-mers in ATATAT with a hash table. Then explain why the locally best next motif need not belong to the best complete motif set.
practice: Split the reads ATAT and TATA between two workers. Count 2-mers within each read, then combine counts by key. Why should no k-mer cross the boundary between these separate reads? For independent motif-search restarts, what can run concurrently and what must be combined at the end?

readings.title: Breadth-first search
readings.focus: Read about directed graphs, adjacency lists, queues and keeping track of visited nodes.

readings.title: Hash tables
readings.focus: Review the data structure used to map each graph node to its outgoing neighbors.

readings.title: NP-hard problems
readings.focus: Read about decision problems, P, NP, reductions and NP-completeness. Use these definitions to distinguish checking a proposed Hamiltonian path from finding one, and to understand the game's change to an Eulerian formulation.

readings.title: Where to go next
readings.focus: Optional scalability extension: Bloom filters screen k-mer membership with possible false positives; HyperLogLog estimates how many distinct k-mers occur. Both trade exact information for lower memory use.

genome-assembly.connection: How does finding a shortest path differ from finding an Eulerian path? Explain why an assembly walk must track used edges, including duplicate edges, rather than simply mark each node visited.
practice: Describe how to check a proposed Hamiltonian path. Why does fast checking not imply that a fast method for finding one is known? Compare this with constructing an Eulerian path in the game's de Bruijn graph.

For a standard Bloom filter, which answer can rule out a k-mer and which needs verification before accepting an exact match? Why can't a HyperLogLog estimate of distinct k-mers recover their sequences or multiplicities for assembly?

readings.title: Dynamic programming
readings.focus: Focus on the longest common substring and longest common subsequence examples, and what each grid cell represents.

readings.title: Dijkstra's algorithm
readings.focus: For an extension, compare weighted shortest paths with alignment paths. Dijkstra's algorithm requires nonnegative edge weights; alignment grids can be solved in dependency order.

alignment.exercises: 11.2-11.3; for the weighted-path extension, 9.1. Exercise 11.3 asks for a substring, which must be contiguous.
alignment.connection: Use the same pair of strings for a longest common substring grid and a longest common subsequence grid. Explain how the mismatch rule changes and which rule allows letters to be skipped.

readings.title: Dynamic programming
readings.focus: Review how a table reuses smaller solutions. Apply that idea to one cell per hidden state and observation position.

readings.title: Recursion
readings.focus: Review base cases and recursive calls before comparing path enumeration with a dynamic programming table.

hmm.connection: For one destination state, write the contribution from each possible predecessor. Why does the forward algorithm sum these contributions while Viterbi takes their maximum? These readings provide the dynamic programming background; they do not introduce HMMs.

readings.title: Trees
readings.focus: Focus on tree structure and depth-first search, then connect recursive traversal to paths in a phylogenetic tree.

readings.title: Recursion
readings.focus: Review the call stack and base cases for algorithms that remove a leaf, solve a smaller tree and restore the leaf.

readings.title: Balanced trees
readings.focus: For an extension, study how height affects lookup. These are search trees; balancing a tree is not a method for inferring evolutionary relationships.

readings.title: Where to go next
readings.focus: Optional implementation extension: UPGMA repeatedly selects a closest pair. A min-heap can organize candidate merges, provided entries for retired clusters are discarded and distances to each new cluster are inserted.

evolutionary-trees.connection: Sketch a tree with four labeled leaves and weighted edges. Trace its unique path between two leaves and add the edge weights. Explain why rotating a search tree is different from reconstructing a tree that preserves biological distances.
practice: In UPGMA, merge clusters A and B into M. Which queued pairs are now invalid, which distances between surviving clusters stay valid, and which new distances must be inserted? Explain how cluster sizes enter the new distances.

readings.title: K-nearest neighbors
readings.focus: Focus on features, distance, normalization and choosing k. KNN predicts from labeled neighbors; k-means clustering learns centers from unlabeled points.

readings.title: Greedy algorithms
readings.focus: For an extension, use locally chosen moves and approximation to think about farthest-first initialization and the limits of local improvement.

readings.title: Where to go next
readings.focus: Optional implementation extension: use a min-heap to organize closest-pair candidates in average-linkage hierarchical clustering. Each merge creates new distances and makes entries involving retired clusters obsolete.

clustering.connection: For points described by gene expression and sequence length, predict how changing the units of sequence length changes nearest neighbors and cluster assignments. What does k count in KNN, and what does it count in k-means?
practice: After merging A and B into M in average-linkage clustering, identify the heap entries to invalidate and the distances to compute. How could you recognize and skip an obsolete entry when it reaches the top? Explain why an unchanged pair of surviving clusters keeps its distance.

readings.title: Introduction to algorithms
readings.focus: Review binary search and Big O notation as preparation for searching a sorted suffix array.

readings.title: Quicksort
readings.focus: Review sorting and divide and conquer, then consider the cost of comparing suffixes instead of single numbers.

readings.title: Trees
readings.focus: For an extension, read the Huffman coding section as another use of structure in compression. It is separate from the Burrows–Wheeler transform and backward search.

readings.title: Selection sort
readings.focus: Focus on the memory and data-structure sections and exercises 2.2-2.5. Random access and insertion costs help explain the choice of representation for a suffix index.

readings.title: Where to go next
readings.focus: A word-to-location index becomes a k-mer-to-genome-position index. Compare explicit occurrence lists with the suffix-array intervals used in read mapping.

burrows-wheeler.connection: Why do all suffixes beginning with the same pattern form one interval in a sorted suffix array? Explain what binary search saves and why comparing a pattern with a suffix can take more than one character comparison.
practice: Why does binary search benefit from an array's random access? Explain the extra work if a linked list must be walked to reach each midpoint. Which representation would you choose for a static suffix index?
Build a 2-mer-to-position index for GATAGACA, using positions starting at 0. Use it to locate GACA. What extra checking is needed when the query is longer than an indexed k-mer?

readings.title: K-nearest neighbors
readings.focus: Focus on features, weighted recommendations, regression and the overview of training a model. These are useful analogies for representations and weighted values; the chapter does not teach attention or transformers.

readings.title: Quicksort
readings.focus: Use this section to reason about the cost of comparing every query with every key.

transformers.connection: Compare weighting a recommender's ratings with weighting values in attention. Which weights depend on the current query? If every one of n positions attends to every position, how many query-key scores are computed, and what happens when n doubles?
